examples.question_text: A rectangular prism has a top face with edges $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$. Find the diagonal $d$ across this face. Give an exact answer, then round to $2$ decimal places.
A cone has perpendicular height $7\text{ cm}$ and base radius $3\text{ cm}$. Find its slant height $s$, rounded to $1$ decimal place.
A cylinder has diameter $12\text{ cm}$ and height $17\text{ cm}$. Find the length $L$ of the longest thin straight rod that fits inside it, rounded to $1$ decimal place.
A cone has perpendicular height $10\text{ cm}$ and slant height $14\text{ cm}$. Find its base diameter, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

A cylinder has base radius $4\text{ cm}$. Its longest thin straight rod is $19\text{ cm}$ long, joining opposite points on the two end rims. Find the cylinder's length $l$, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

A pyramid has a rectangular base measuring $8\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$. Its apex $E$ is directly above the centre $O$ of the base. Each apex-to-corner edge is $13\text{ cm}$. Find the perpendicular height $h$, rounded to $1$ decimal place.

methods.description: Identify the right-angled triangle on a rectangular face and add the squares of its edges to find the diagonal; retain an exact value or round as requested.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 45–71, face-diagonal definition and worked example

methods.description: Use the cone's radius and perpendicular height as the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle to find its slant height.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 170–177, Foundation question 2 and image18.png

methods.description: Use the cylinder's diameter and axial length as the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle to find the longest rod.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 180–189, Foundation question 3 and image19.png

methods.description: Subtract the squared perpendicular height from the squared slant height to find the radius, then double it to obtain the diameter.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 235–240, Mastery question 6(a), image23.png panel a

methods.description: Convert radius to diameter where needed, then subtract its square from the squared diagonal rod length to find the cylinder's axial length.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 235–240, Mastery question 6(b), image23.png panel b

methods.description: Find the base diagonal, halve it to obtain the centre-to-corner distance, then use the apex-to-corner edge as the hypotenuse to find the perpendicular height. The rectangular-base adaptation is explicitly approved in the supplied assessment acceptance.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Trigonometry C 1_3D Trigonometry.md lines 303–315, Mastery question 10 and images26.png–27.png; supplied accepted rectangular-base adaptation

coverage.summary: Authored six worked examples covering every distinct retained assessment method. Assessments were read only for method classification and were neither changed nor re-audited. Each example separates question and solution fields, includes editable planar section or triangle diagrams, and keeps derived annotations in the solution. Working uses complete left-hand sides, so no phantom equals gutters are needed. Plain solution prose and mathematics inherit the supplied renderer's blue styling; diagram ink remains black. Final-size rendering and independent review of the new examples remain coordinator stages.

examples.derivation: The face edges are perpendicular: d² = 7² + 10² = 149. Thus d = √149 cm ≈ 12.21 cm. The solution triangle correctly labels both edges and the diagonal.
The radius and perpendicular height form the shorter sides: s² = 3² + 7² = 58. Thus s = √58 cm ≈ 7.6 cm. The right-angle marker and side annotations agree.
The axial section has width equal to the diameter, 12 cm, and height 17 cm. Its diagonal satisfies L² = 144 + 289 = 433, giving L ≈ 20.8 cm. The rectangle and rod annotations agree.
The slant height is the hypotenuse: r² = 14² − 10² = 96. The diameter is 2√96 cm ≈ 19.60 cm. The solution correctly retains the exact radius before doubling.
The diameter is 2 × 4 = 8 cm. The axial-section diagonal is 19 cm, so l² = 19² − 8² = 297 and l ≈ 17.23 cm. The rectangle assigns the diameter and axial length to the correct sides.

The rectangular base diagonal is √(8² + 6²) = 10 cm. Its centre-to-corner distance is 5 cm. Since the apex is directly above the centre, h² = 13² − 5² = 144, giving h = 12.0 cm. Both planar diagrams correctly represent these triangles.

review.summary: All six distinct assessed methods have mapped example coverage. All 25 assessment locators are mapped individually; accepted assessment mathematics was not re-audited. The supplied source supports the methods, including the explicitly approved rectangular-base pyramid adaptation. There were no existing examples to retain or audit. New calculations, annotations and planar geometry pass independent review. Complete left-hand sides make phantom equals gutters unnecessary. Separate fields, single-dollar aligned mathematics and plain prose comply with the supplied renderer contract. Final-size rendering and label verification remain for the coordinator's visual stage.
